parts.latex: Calculate the mean and the range of goals that Sophie scored throughout the season.
Use calculations to determine whether any of Sophie's scores are outliers.

criteria: Correct mean or correct range, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The quartiles of the data are
$$Q_1 = 5, \quad Q_3 = 11$$
so the interquartile range is
$$IQR = 11 - 5 = 6$$
Outliers lie below $Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR &= 5 - 1.5\times 6 = -4 \\ Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 11 + 1.5\times 6 = 20 \end{aligned}$$
Since $24 > 20$, 24 is an outlier.
criteria: Finds the outlier boundaries $-4$ and $20$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The five-number summary of a dataset is given.

Lowest score $= 1$

Lower quartile $(Q_1) = 4$

Median $(Q_2) = 7$

Upper quartile $(Q_3) = 10$

Highest score $= 20$

Is 20 an outlier? Justify your answer with calculations.

solutions.latex:
The interquartile range is
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 10 - 4 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
An outlier lies above $Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 10 + 1.5\times 6 \\ &= 19 \end{aligned}$$
Since $20 > 19$, 20 is an outlier.
criteria: Attempts to use $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$, or calculates the interquartile range

parts.latex:
The heights, in centimetres, of 10 players on a basketball team are shown.

$$170, 180, 185, 188, 192, 193, 193, 194, 196, 202$$

Is the height of the shortest player on the team considered an outlier? Justify your answer with calculations.

solutions.latex:
The lower and upper quartiles are $Q_1=185$ and $Q_3=194$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= 194-185 \\ &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
A value is an outlier if it is less than
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1-1.5\times IQR &= 185-1.5\times 9 \\ &= 171.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $170<171.5$, the shortest height is considered an outlier.
criteria: Calculates the interquartile range, or equivalent merit
Finds a quartile, or equivalent merit

6042.stem:
The number of cars parked in a carpark is recorded each day for thirteen days. The dataset is listed in ascending order:

$$12, 15, 15, 17, 19, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30 \text{ and } m.$$

parts.latex: What is the interquartile range of this dataset?
What is the greatest value of $m$ such that this dataset has no outlier?

solutions.latex:
With 13 scores, the lower half is the first 6 scores and the upper half is the last 6 scores.

The lower quartile is the average of the 3rd and 4th scores:
$$Q_1 = \dfrac{15+17}{2} = 16$$
The upper quartile is the average of the 10th and 11th scores:
$$Q_3 = \dfrac{27+28}{2} = 27.5$$
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 27.5 - 16 \\ &= 11.5 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the lower or upper quartile, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
An outlier lies above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper bound} &= 27.5 + 1.5 \times 11.5 \\ &= 44.75 \end{aligned}$$
Since the number of cars is a whole number, the greatest value of $m$ with no outlier is $44$.
$$\therefore\ m = 44$$
criteria: Attempts to find the upper bound, or equivalent merit

6115.stem:
Mike completes ten spelling tests and receives the following scores:

$$10, 11, 11, 12, 14, 14, 16, 19, 19, 20$$

parts.latex: What is Mike's standard deviation? Give your answer correct to one decimal place
If Mike scores 5 in the next spelling test, will it be considered an outlier? Justify your answer with mathematical calculations.

solutions.latex:
From the ordered data:
$$Q_1 = 11, \quad Q_3 = 19, \quad \text{IQR} = 8$$
Lower outlier boundary:
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR} &= 11 - 1.5 \times 8 \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $5 > -1$, a score of $5$ is not below the boundary.
$$\therefore\ \text{not an outlier}$$
criteria: Finds the quartiles and IQR, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The number of thorns on a variety of rose bushes were recorded in a stem-and-leaf plot.

The leaf from the first entry is shown as “$x$”.

\extable{717_q26_t1}

What is the largest value of $x$ for which this entry could be considered an outlier?

solutions.latex:
From the stem-and-leaf plot:
$$\begin{aligned}Q_1&=36\\Q_2&=42\\Q_3&=51\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}IQR&=51-36\\&=15\end{aligned}$$
An outlier lies below the lower fence $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Lower fence}&=36-(1.5\times 15)\\&=13.5\end{aligned}$$
So an outlier is less than 13.5.
$$\therefore\ x=3$$
criteria: Finds the lower fence, or equivalent merit
Finds the interquartile range, or equivalent merit
Finds the quartiles, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The heights of students in a class are represented in the boxplot below.

\exfigure{850_q6_1}

A new student, who will become the tallest member, is joining the class.

What is the maximum height the new student can be in order to not be classified as an outlier?

solutions.latex:
A student is an outlier if their height is above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Upper bound}&=Q_3+1.5\times IQR\\&=170+1.5\times(170-155)\\&=192.5\end{aligned}$$
Any student taller than 192.5 cm is an outlier.

Hence the maximum height is 192.5 cm, option B.

850_q6_1.notes: Box plot: min 147, Q1 155, median 160, Q3 170, max 180 at 0.9pt (rule 9), scale 140 to 190 with ticks every 5, 'Height (cm)' title. Rules 1, 2, 3, 9.

parts.latex:
A set of data has a lower quartile of 36 and an upper quartile of 48.

What is the maximum possible range if there are no outliers in the data set?

solutions.latex:
The interquartile range is

$$\text{IQR} = 48 - 36 = 12$$
A score is an outlier if it lies outside the fences

$$\begin{aligned} \text{lower fence} &= Q_1 - 1.5\times \text{IQR} = 36 - 18 = 18 \\ \text{upper fence} &= Q_3 + 1.5\times \text{IQR} = 48 + 18 = 66 \end{aligned}$$
With no outliers, all scores lie between $18$ and $66$. The range is largest when the minimum is $18$ and the maximum is $66$.

$$\text{Range} = 66 - 18 = 48$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum possible range} = 48$$
criteria: Finds both the upper and lower fences, or equivalent merit
Finds the interquartile range of $12$, or equivalent merit

meta.generated_note: Uses the 1.5 x IQR outlier rule.

6591.stem:
David recorded the duration of his phone calls (in minutes) over a day. The results are shown on the dot plot.

\exfigure{821_q34_1}

figures.cap: dot plot of call duration in minutes

parts.latex: What was the interquartile range of David's calls?
Justify, using calculations, that David's twelve-minute call was an outlier.

solutions.latex:
From the dot plot:

$$Q_2 = 3,\quad Q_1 = 2,\quad Q_3 = 5$$

$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 5 - 2 \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$

A value is an outlier if it is above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR$.

$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR &= 5 + 1.5 \times 3 \\ &= 9.5 \end{aligned}$$

Since $12 > 9.5$,

$$\therefore\ 12 \text{ is an outlier.}$$
criteria: Finds the upper boundary, or equivalent merit

821_q34_1.notes: Dot plot with counts 1:1, 2:5, 3:4, 4:4, 5:3, 6:1, 12:1, drawn as grey-filled outlined ellipses at the crop's grid (48.8 px per minute, 79 px per call). Axes have ticks and filled arrows, and both axis titles are kept, the y title rotated. The crop's sans font is replaced by the house font (rule 19). The y tick numbers are upright; in the crop they are rotated, which is a scan artefact. The overlay is just under 0.85 only because the fonts differ.

parts.latex:
On a rail station, a train is scheduled to arrive at 9:00am each morning.

The following data shows the times the train arrived on seven consecutive days.

9:03am, 9:04am, 9:02am, 9:11am, 9:02am, 9:03am, 9:01am

With the aid of calculation, determine whether the arrival time of 9:11am could be considered an outlier for the presented data.

solutions.latex:
Order the data (minutes after 9:00):
$$1,\ 2,\ 2,\ 3,\ 3,\ 4,\ 11$$
The quartiles are $Q_1=2$ and $Q_3=4$.
$$IQR=4-2=2 \text{ minutes}$$
Upper fence:
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times IQR &= 4+1.5\times 2 \\ &= 7 \text{ minutes, that is } 9{:}07 \end{aligned}$$
Since 9:11 is greater than 9:07, it is an outlier.
criteria: Finds the upper fence, or equivalent merit

6662.stem:
In a small business, the seven employees earn the following wages per week:

$\$450,\ \$735,\ \$780,\ \$885,\ \$990,\ \$1\,020,\ \$1\,455$

parts.latex: Is the wage of \$1 455 an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations

Each employee will receive a \$40 pay increase.

What effect will this have on the standard deviation. Give a reason for your answer.

solutions.latex:
The data are in order, with $n = 7$. The median is $\$885$, so the lower half is $450, 735, 780$ and the upper half is $990, 1020, 1455$.
$$Q_1 = 735, \qquad Q_3 = 1020$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= 1020 - 735 \\ &= 285 \end{aligned}$$
An outlier lies above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper fence} &= 1020 + 1.5\times 285 \\ &= 1447.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1455 > 1447.5$, the wage of $\$1455$ is an outlier.
criteria: Finds $Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the IQR, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: Quartiles as medians of halves; fence 1447.5 < 1455.

solutions.latex:
The standard deviation will not change.

Adding \$40 to every wage shifts every score and the mean by \$40, so each score's distance from the mean is unchanged. The spread of the data is the same.

meta.self_check: Standard property of translation of data.

figures.cap: back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot, male and female

solutions.latex:
There are 30 scores, so the median is the mean of the 15th and 16th scores.

$$\text{Median}=11$$

$$Q_1=\text{8th score}=8,\qquad Q_3=\text{22nd score}=18$$

$$IQR=18-8=10$$

Upper fence:

$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times IQR &= 18+1.5\times 10 \\ &= 33 \end{aligned}$$

Since $71>33$, 71 is an outlier.
criteria: Finds the $IQR$ and the upper fence, or equivalent merit
